summary: Defines the syntax of Uniform Resource Names, persistent location-independent identifiers under the urn URI scheme. It specifies how to decide if two URNs are equivalent, how to define a URN namespace, and how namespace identifiers are registered with IANA. It replaces RFC 2141 and RFC 3406.

plainLanguage.summary: A URN is a permanent name for a thing. Unlike a web address, it does not say where the thing is, so it keeps working when the thing moves. This document defines the shape of a URN, says when two URNs are the same name, and explains how an organisation registers its own URN namespace.

questions: how to register a urn namespace
subtitle: Names that keep pointing at the same thing for as long as it exists, rather than at a place that can move.

tldr.problem: A URL says where something is now, so it breaks when the thing moves. Many things need a name that survives a move, a rename or a change of owner.
tldr.mechanism: A URN is a URI under the urn scheme that names a resource permanently. The syntax gives it a namespace identifier and a namespace-specific string, and the RFC defines when two URNs count as the same name and how a new namespace is registered with IANA.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8141 obsoletes RFC 2141 and RFC 3406, which together defined URN syntax and namespace registration. Names registered under the older rules stay valid.

facts.label: Case handling
facts.value: Scheme and NID are case insensitive; NSS is case sensitive by default

today: RFC 8141 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2017. It obsoletes RFC 2141 and RFC 3406; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What a URN Is
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name is a Uniform Resource Identifier that is assigned under the urn URI scheme and a particular URN namespace, with the intent that the URN will be a persistent, location-independent resource identifier. A URN namespace is a collection of such URNs, each of which is unique, assigned in a consistent and managed way, and assigned according to a common definition. Some URN namespaces create names that exist only as URNs, while others assign URNs based on names already created in other identifier systems, such as ISBNs, ISSNs or RFC numbers.

The assignment of URNs is done by an organization, or in some cases by an algorithm or other automated process, that has been formally delegated a URN namespace within the urn scheme. A URN in the example namespace might be of the form urn:example:foo.

The document rests on two key assumptions: that assignment of a URN is a managed process, and that the space of URN namespaces is itself managed. While other URI schemes may allow resource identifiers to be freely chosen and assigned, that is not the case for URNs. Syntactic correctness of a name starting with urn is not sufficient to make it a URN: the namespace identifier has to be registered under the rules of this document, and the rest of the assigned-name portion has to be generated under the rules of the registered namespace. All URN namespaces and URNs that were valid under the earlier specifications remain valid, and the intent throughout is to define URNs so that, wherever practical, their parsing, handling and resolution can be independent of the namespace they were assigned in.
sections.plainLanguage: Unlike a web address, a URN does not say where the thing lives. It is issued by an organisation that promises never to hand the same name to something else, and it is meant to keep working for decades.

sections.title: The Terms This Document Uses
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes several terms that are often mixed up. A URN is a URI using the urn scheme with the properties of a name, and the term applies to the entire URI including its optional components. A locator is an identifier that provides a means of accessing a resource. An identifier system is a managed collection of names, called non-URN identifier systems when they sit outside the URN world. A URN namespace is an identifier system associated with a URN namespace identifier, or NID. The NSS is the URN-namespace-specific part of a URN. The assigned-name is the combination of the urn scheme, the NID and the NSS, and is therefore a substring of a URN if that URN carries additional components.

The RFC deliberately does not define the word name, since it is used informally in practice and RFC 3986 uses it in several different senses that would conflict with the terms used here. Resolution is used in the sense of the original architectural principles for URNs: the act of supplying services related to the identified resource, such as translating the persistent URN into one or more current locators, delivering metadata about the resource, or even delivering a representation of the resource such as a document. The document uses the terms resource, identifier, identify, dereference, representation and metadata roughly as the URI specification defines them.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is careful about words. A URN is the whole identifier, an NID says which organisation issued it, and the NSS is the part that organisation chose. Resolution means turning the name into something useful, such as a current address or a document.

sections.title: The Syntax of a URN
sections.content:
The syntax is given in Augmented Backus-Naur Form, with the alphanum, fragment and pchar rules taken from the URI specification so that the relationship with URI syntax is visible. A URN is written as urn, a colon, a namespace identifier, a colon and a namespace specific string, optionally followed by the r-component and q-component and then the f-component.

The NID syntax is (alphanum) 0*30(ldh) (alphanum), where ldh is an alphanumeric character or a hyphen, so a namespace identifier is case insensitive, for example ISBN and isbn are equivalent. Characters outside the ASCII range are not permitted in NIDs and no encoding mechanism for them is supported. The NSS is a string that is unique within its namespace and conforms to the definition of that namespace. The combination of the NID, which is unique across the whole urn scheme, and the NSS, which is unique within its namespace, ensures that the resulting URN is globally unique.

The NSS allows several characters that earlier specifications did not permit. In particular the slash character is now allowed, which effectively makes it possible to encapsulate hierarchical names from non-URN identifier systems, so a name such as 1/406/47452/2 becomes urn:example:1/406/47452/2. Names that are valid in another identifier system might still contain characters that URN syntax does not allow, and such a name is not a valid URN until it has been translated into an NSS that conforms to the rules of that namespace. Software that is not aware of namespace-specific canonicalization and encoding rules MUST NOT construct URNs from such a name. Characters outside the ASCII range must be encoded in UTF-8 and then percent-encoded as the URI specification requires, and URN namespaces SHOULD NOT allow such characters unless the nature of the namespace makes them necessary, because URNs should stay stable as protocols evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN reads as urn, then the namespace, then the name that namespace uses. The namespace part is short and case insensitive, and the name part may contain slashes so that names from older systems can be carried over unchanged.

sections.title: The Three Optional Components
sections.content:
The syntax includes three optional components: the r-component, the q-component and the f-component. Each has a distinct role that does not depend on any particular URN or namespace, and the intent is that clients handle them uniformly for all URNs. They MAY be used with URNs from existing namespaces, whether or not a namespace explicitly supports them, though the behaviour of a URN containing components that are undefined or meaningless for a particular namespace is not defined.

The r-component is intended for passing parameters to URN resolution services, and it has no syntactic counterpart in any other known URI scheme. The sequence ?+ introduces it, and it ends with a ?= sequence or a number sign, or runs to the end of the URN. It is reserved for future use, and the RFC says r-components SHOULD NOT be used before their semantics have been standardized. The q-component is intended for passing parameters to the named resource or to a system that can supply the requested service. It has the same syntax as the URI query component but is introduced by ?=, and for a URN that resolves to a locator the semantics are identical to those of the query component of that URI, so a resolver returns a URI that is a locator by copying the q-component into the query component. The f-component is intended to be interpreted by the client as a specification for a location within the named resource. It has the same syntax as the URI fragment component, is introduced by the number sign, and ends at the end of the URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Three optional pieces can follow a URN. One asks the resolver something, one carries parameters for the thing being named, and one points at a part of it, such as a chapter of a book.

sections.title: Deciding Whether Two URNs Are the Same
sections.content:
For purposes such as caching it is often desirable to know whether two URNs are the same. Two URNs are URN-equivalent if their assigned-name portions are octet-by-octet equal after three normalizations: the URI scheme urn is converted to lower case, the NID is converted to lower case, and any percent-encoded characters in the NSS are converted to upper case for the digits A-F. Percent-encoded characters MUST NOT be decoded, so percent-encoding normalization is not applied as part of the comparison. If an r-component, q-component or f-component is included in a URN, it MUST be ignored for the purpose of determining URN-equivalence.

Namespace definitions MAY include additional rules, such as case insensitivity of the NSS or parts of it. Such rules MUST always have the effect of eliminating some of the false negatives the base procedure produces and MUST NOT result in treating two URNs as different when the base procedure says they are equivalent.

The RFC's examples show the rules at work. Because the scheme and NID are case insensitive, urn:example:a123,z456, URN:example:a123,z456 and urn:EXAMPLE:a123,z456 are equivalent, and so are those three with ?+abc, ?=xyz or #789 appended, because the optional components are ignored. Because the slash and everything after it in the NSS counts, urn:example:a123,z456/foo and urn:example:a123,z456/bar are not equivalent to each other or to the earlier ones. Because percent-encoded sequences are not decoded, urn:example:a123%2Cz456 is equivalent only to itself in different case. Because characters in the NSS other than percent-encoded sequences are case sensitive, urn:example:A123,z456 is not equivalent to the first three. And a URN that looks the same on screen but uses a Cyrillic letter, urn:example:%D0%B0123,z456, is not equivalent to the Latin-letter version.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names are the same if they differ only in the case of the urn scheme and the namespace, or in the case of the letters inside a percent-encoded sequence. Anything after the slash counts, and the three optional pieces at the end do not.

sections.title: Defining and Registering a URN Namespace
sections.content:
Because the space of URN namespaces is itself managed, the definition of a namespace has to cover six things: the purpose of the namespace, the syntax of the URNs assigned within it, the process for assigning them, the security implications, any interoperability issues, and optionally the process for resolving them. The registration template in Appendix A has a section for each, and this document explains what belongs in them.

There are two kinds of namespace. A formal URN namespace provides benefit to some subset of users on the Internet, and the organisation running it should show organisational stability and the ability to maintain the namespace for a long time, competence in URN assignment, and a commitment never to reassign existing URNs and to let old URNs stay valid. A formal namespace establishes a particular NID, which MUST NOT be an already registered NID, MUST NOT start with urn-, which is reserved for informal namespaces, MUST be more than two characters long, MUST NOT start with two letters followed by a hyphen, which is reserved for possible country-code-based namespaces, and MUST NOT start with the string X-. An informal URN namespace is a full-fledged namespace, but the registrant does not choose the NID: IANA assigns the string urn- followed by digits, such as urn-7.

The basic registration policy for namespaces is Expert Review. The applicant fills out the template, sends it to the urn@ietf.org discussion list, revises it if the reviewers ask for changes, and then the Designated Experts approve it and IANA registers the NID, unless standardization is anticipated, in which case the experts prepare a report for the standards approval body and IANA waits for its directions. A separate fast track exists for URN namespaces that come from a recognized standards development organization or scientific society, where the template is filled out, a specification reflecting the external standards is required, the reviews are advisory, and the body asks IANA to complete the registration when it is ready. The discussion list urn-nid@apps.ietf.org from the earlier specification is discontinued and replaced by urn@ietf.org.
sections.plainLanguage: An organisation that wants its own URN namespace fills in a template and asks IANA for a short code such as example. The review is by people appointed for the job, and organisations that speak for a whole field can go through a faster route.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The definition of a URN namespace has to account for potential security and privacy issues related to the assignment, use and resolution of names, and the RFC notes that some URN resolvers might assign special meaning to certain characters in the NSS. The registration template asks applicants to describe such issues, with examples that include the consequences of producing false negatives and false positives when comparing URNs for equivalence, leakage of private information when names are communicated on the public Internet, and the potential for directory harvesting.

In most cases URN namespaces provide a way to declare public information. Those declarations normally have a low security profile, but there is always the danger of spoofing and of providing misinformation, so information in these declarations ought to be taken as advisory rather than authoritative.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN usually states something public, so it carries little security weight on its own. The danger is that a name is faked or that publishing one leaks something private, which is why the template asks about both.

viz.caption: THE URN GRAMMAR FROM SECTION 2 OF THE RFC

data.title: URN syntax
data.code:
namestring    = assigned-name
                [ rq-components ]
                [ "#" f-component ]
assigned-name = "urn" ":" NID ":" NSS
NID           = (alphanum) 0*30(ldh) (alphanum)
ldh           = alphanum / "-"
NSS           = pchar *(pchar / "/")
rq-components = [ "?+" r-component ]
                [ "?=" q-component ]
r-component   = pchar *( pchar / "/" / "?" )
q-component   = pchar *( pchar / "/" / "?" )
f-component   = fragment

items.title: r-component
items.text: Parameters for the resolution service, introduced by ?+. Reserved for future standardization.

items.title: q-component
items.text: Parameters for the named resource, introduced by ?=. Copied into the query of a locator on resolution.

items.title: f-component
items.text: A location within the named resource, introduced by #. Same syntax as a URI fragment.
